title: ₹1,600 Crore. Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman. Ranbir as Ram. India's Biggest Film Just Got Real.
excerpt: Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana cleared CinemaCon, locked its Diwali date, and revealed Ranbir Kapoor's dual role. Here's everything the diaspora needs to know.
body:
The numbers alone make you sit up. **₹1,600 crore** across two parts — the single most expensive Indian film franchise ever green-lit. **Nitesh Tiwari** directing, fresh off *Dangal*, the highest-grossing Bollywood film in history. **Ranbir Kapoor** as Lord Ram. **Sai Pallavi** as Sita. **Yash** — the man who turned *KGF* into a national event — as Ravana. **Sunny Deol** as Hanuman. And the score? **A.R. Rahman** and **Hans Zimmer**. Together.

**Ramayana** isn't just a film. It's an industry-defining event, and it's arriving this Diwali.

## What CinemaCon Revealed

When producer **Namit Malhotra** presented Ramayana at CinemaCon — the global exhibition industry's most important gathering — the message was unmissable. This wasn't positioned as an Indian film hoping for a few international screens. Exclusive footage was showcased alongside Hollywood tentpoles. Private screenings targeted distributors across North America, Europe, Latin America, and Australia. The film was placed where *Avatar* and *Avengers* sit, and the international industry reportedly paid attention.

> "Global audiences are now actively seeking fresh stories and new cultural perspectives." — Namit Malhotra, Producer

Yash added context at the event, revealing that Part 1 may explore parallel character arcs with limited direct interaction between the leads early on — a layered storytelling approach that builds toward the central confrontation. This isn't a straight retelling. This is a cinematic epic structured more like *The Lord of the Rings* than any mythological film India has attempted before.

## Ranbir's Dual Role and the Six-Hour Vision

In an interview following the release of the first teaser — which drew overwhelmingly positive reactions — **Ranbir Kapoor** confirmed two revelations the industry had been whispering about. First: he plays a dual role, both **Lord Rama** and **Lord Parashurama**, with the teaser offering a glimpse of the latter. Second: the two parts will together run over **six hours**, suggesting a narrative scope closer to Peter Jackson than T-Series.

The teaser made an impression. Ranbir's look as Ram was praised for its spiritual dignity, the background score — Rahman and Zimmer's first joint effort — delivered the kind of goosebump-inducing orchestral sweep Indian cinema rarely attempts, and the VFX by **DNEG**, an 8-time Oscar-winning studio, looked genuinely competitive with global blockbusters.

Ranbir shared something personal that explains why the performance carries weight: he had initially refused the role, feeling the responsibility was too enormous. When his daughter Raha was born, his perspective changed. "Playing Lord Rama is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," he said.

## The Biggest Indian Film Ever Made — By the Numbers

Part 1's budget stands at approximately **₹900 crore**, with Part 2 estimated at **₹700 crore** — leveraging existing digital assets and sets from the first installment. The distribution deal is reportedly being negotiated at around **₹450 crore**, the highest in Indian film history. Part 1 currently targets an **October 30, 2026** release — a week before Diwali — to build word-of-mouth before the festive rush. Part 2 follows Diwali 2027.

The film has been shot using **IMAX-certified cameras**, earning the coveted "Filmed For IMAX" distinction that places it alongside productions like *Dune* and *Oppenheimer*. An official trailer is expected in July, with reports suggesting the "Ramayana: The Introduction" promo will premiere at a Mumbai multiplex around July 3.

## Why the Diaspora Should Be Watching

For NRIs, Ramayana is shaping up to be the cultural event of the decade. It's the rare Indian film that will command premium screens worldwide — IMAX runs in the US, UK, Canada, Australia — not as an "Indian language" release tucked into a matinee slot, but as a global event film. The combination of Rahman's spiritual compositions with Zimmer's orchestral grandeur was designed with exactly this audience in mind: people who carry the mythology in their bones but expect Hollywood-grade spectacle.

The cast is tailored for pan-India and global appeal. Ranbir brings Bollywood's smouldering intensity. Yash commands the mass Southern audience. Sai Pallavi offers the kind of luminous screen presence that crosses language barriers without effort. And Sunny Deol as Hanuman is the kind of casting that makes you grin just thinking about it.

The shooting for Part 2 is already 50 per cent complete — Ranbir confirmed the schedule expects to wrap before Part 1 hits theaters. This isn't a franchise hoping to get a greenlight. Both chapters are being built simultaneously, with a confidence in the material that borders on historic.

This Diwali, when the lights come up in theaters from New Jersey to New Delhi, Ramayana won't just be a movie. It'll be a pilgrimage.
